claim: Male infertility affects 5–10% of men.
source: Male infertility is a prevalent condition, affecting 5–10% of men.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of male infertility in the general population, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The Y lineage R1a1-M458 is reported at >20% frequency in several European populations.
source: The Y lineage R1a1-M458, reported at >20% frequency in several European populations, carries a fixed ~1.6 Mb r2/r3 inversion, destabilizing the AZFc region and predisposing to large recurrent microdeletions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to published data on Y-chromosomal haplogroup frequencies.

claim: The Y lineage R1a1-M458 carries a fixed ~1.6 Mb r2/r3 inversion.
source: The Y lineage R1a1-M458, reported at >20% frequency in several European populations, carries a fixed ~1.6 Mb r2/r3 inversion, destabilizing the AZFc region and predisposing to large recurrent microdeletions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genetic analysis of Y chromosomes.

claim: The r2/r3 inversion destabilizes the AZFc region and predisposes to large recurrent microdeletions.
source: The Y lineage R1a1-M458, reported at >20% frequency in several European populations, carries a fixed ~1.6 Mb r2/r3 inversion, destabilizing the AZFc region and predisposing to large recurrent microdeletions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed association between the inversion and subsequent deletions in the study data.

claim: Complex rearrangements combining r2/r3 inversion with deletions were significantly enriched among severe oligozoospermia cases.
source: Such complex rearrangements were significantly enriched among severe oligozoospermia cases.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study comparing patient and control groups.

claim: The carrier vs non-carrier risk for spermatogenic failure was increased 8.6-fold (p=6.0×10−4).
source: The carrier vs non-carrier risk for spermatogenic failure was increased 8.6-fold (p=6.0×10−4).
evidence: This is a quantitative statistical result from the study's association analysis.

claim: The diagnosis of male factor infertility due to abnormal semen parameters concerns ~10% of men.
source: The diagnosis of male factor infertility due to abnormal semen parameters concerns ~10% of men (Jungwirth et al., 2012; Datta et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In today's andrology workup, ~60% of patients with spermatogenic failure remain idiopathic.
source: In today's andrology workup, ~60% of patients with spermatogenic failure remain idiopathic (Punab et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about clinical practice supported by a citation.

claim: Karyotype abnormalities are found in up to 17% of patients with spermatogenic failure.
source: Among the known causes, the most widely considered genetic factors are karyotype abnormalities (up to 17% of patients) and recurrent de novo microdeletions of the Y-chromosomal Azoospermia Factor a (AZFa) (~0.8 Mb), AZFb (~6.2 Mb), and AZFc (~3.5 Mb) regions (2–10%) (Punab et al., 2017; Olesen et al., 2017; Tüttelmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This prevalence estimate is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Recurrent de novo microdeletions of Y-chromosomal AZF regions occur in 2–10% of patients with spermatogenic failure.
source: Among the known causes, the most widely considered genetic factors are karyotype abnormalities (up to 17% of patients) and recurrent de novo microdeletions of the Y-chromosomal Azoospermia Factor a (AZFa) (~0.8 Mb), AZFb (~6.2 Mb), and AZFc (~3.5 Mb) regions (2–10%) (Punab et al., 2017; Olesen et al., 2017; Tüttelmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This prevalence estimate is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Testing for AZF deletions has been strongly recommended in the diagnostic workup for infertility patients with sperm concentration of <5 × 106/ml for more than 15 years.
source: For more than 15 years, testing for AZF deletions has been strongly recommended in the diagnostic workup for infertility patients with sperm concentration of <5 × 106/ml (ASRM, 2015; Krausz et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement about clinical guidelines is supported by citations.

claim: Most deletion carriers represent patients with either azoospermia or cryptozoospermia.
source: Most deletion carriers represent patients with either azoospermia (no sperm) or cryptozoospermia (>0–1 million sperm/ejaculate) (Punab et al., 2017; Kohn et al., 2019; Stahl et al., 2010).
evidence: This clinical observation is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The most prevalent deletion type is AZFc (~80%).
source: The most prevalent deletion type is AZFc (~80%), followed by the loss of AZFa (0.5–4%), AZFb (1–5%), and AZFbc (1–3%) regions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This prevalence data is stated in the text and referenced to Figure 1A.

claim: Excess of recurrent AZFc deletions is promoted by the region's complex genomic structure comprised of long direct and inverted amplicons of nearly identical DNA segments.
source: Excess of recurrent AZFc deletions is promoted by the region's complex genomic structure comprised of long direct and inverted amplicons of nearly identical DNA segments that lead to aberrant meiotic rearrangements in gametogenesis (Kuroda-Kawaguchi et al., 2001; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Figure 1B).
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The AZFc full deletions remove all the multicopy DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes.
source: The AZFc full deletions remove all the multicopy DAZ (deleted in azoospermia 1), BPY2 (basic charge Y-linked 2), and CDY1 (chromodomain Y-linked 1) genes that are expressed in a testis-enriched manner and considered important in spermatogenesis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement about gene content is supported by reference to Figure 1C and established knowledge.

claim: DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes are expressed in a testis-enriched manner and considered important in spermatogenesis.
source: The AZFc full deletions remove all the multicopy DAZ (deleted in azoospermia 1), BPY2 (basic charge Y-linked 2), and CDY1 (chromodomain Y-linked 1) genes that are expressed in a testis-enriched manner and considered important in spermatogenesis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement about gene function is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The gr/gr deletion spans approximately 1.6 Mb.
source: The most prevalent partial deletion types, named after the involved amplicons as g(reen)-r(ed)/g(reen)-r(ed) (lost segment ~1.6 Mb) and b(lue)2/b(lue)3 (~1.8 Mb) reduce the copy number of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes by roughly 50% (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This size estimate is stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The b2/b3 deletion spans approximately 1.8 Mb.
source: The most prevalent partial deletion types, named after the involved amplicons as g(reen)-r(ed)/g(reen)-r(ed) (lost segment ~1.6 Mb) and b(lue)2/b(lue)3 (~1.8 Mb) reduce the copy number of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes by roughly 50% (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This size estimate is stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: gr/gr and b2/b3 deletions reduce the copy number of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes by roughly 50%.
source: The most prevalent partial deletion types, named after the involved amplicons as g(reen)-r(ed)/g(reen)-r(ed) (lost segment ~1.6 Mb) and b(lue)2/b(lue)3 (~1.8 Mb) reduce the copy number of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes by roughly 50% (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement about gene dosage is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: In European populations, the carrier status of the gr/gr deletion increases a risk to low sperm counts ~1.8-fold.
source: In European populations, the carrier status of the gr/gr deletion increases a risk to low sperm counts ~1.8-fold (Rozen et al., 2012; Bansal et al., 2016a; Krausz et al., 2009).
evidence: This risk estimate is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The gr/gr deletion is completely fixed in Y haplogroups D2 and Q1a that are common in Japan and some parts of China.
source: Its more variable effect on spermatogenesis has been shown in Middle Eastern and Asian populations, where the gr/gr deletion is completely fixed in some Y lineages, for example haplogroups D2 and Q1a that are common in Japan and some parts of China (de Carvalho et al., 2006; Teitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement about haplogroup-specific fixation is supported by citations.

claim: The b2/b3 deletion appears to be a risk factor for spermatogenic impairment in several East Asian and African populations.
source: In contrast, the b2/b3 deletion appears to be a risk factor for spermatogenic impairment in several East Asian and African, but not in European or South Asian populations (Bansal et al., 2016b; Colaco and Modi, 2018).
evidence: This population-specific association is supported by citations.

claim: The b2/b3 deletion is not a risk factor for spermatogenic impairment in European or South Asian populations.
source: In contrast, the b2/b3 deletion appears to be a risk factor for spermatogenic impairment in several East Asian and African, but not in European or South Asian populations (Bansal et al., 2016b; Colaco and Modi, 2018).
evidence: This population-specific lack of association is supported by citations.

claim: The b2/b3 deletion is completely fixed in Y haplogroup N3.
source: Notably, the b2/b3 deletion is completely fixed in Y haplogroup N3 that has a high frequency (up to 90% in some populations) in Finno-Ugric-, Baltic-, and some Turkic-speaking people living in Northern Eurasia (Rozen et al., 2012; Fernandes et al., 2004; Ilumäe et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement about haplogroup-specific fixation is supported by citations.

claim: Y haplogroup N3 has a high frequency (up to 90% in some populations) in Finno-Ugric-, Baltic-, and some Turkic-speaking people living in Northern Eurasia.
source: Notably, the b2/b3 deletion is completely fixed in Y haplogroup N3 that has a high frequency (up to 90% in some populations) in Finno-Ugric-, Baltic-, and some Turkic-speaking people living in Northern Eurasia (Rozen et al., 2012; Fernandes et al., 2004; Ilumäe et al., 2016).
evidence: This population frequency data is supported by citations.

claim: There was a statistically significant excess of gr/gr deletions in idiopathic male infertility patients (2.7%) compared to reference cases (1.2%).
source: A statistically significant excess of gr/gr deletions was detected in idiopathic male infertility patients (2.7%; n = 32/1190) compared to reference cases (1.2%; n = 14/1134) (Fisher's exact test, p=0.016; odds ratio [OR] = 2.2 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.2–4.2]) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's comparison of patient and control groups.

claim: The highest frequency of gr/gr deletion carriers (6.8%) was detected in cryptozoospermia cases.
source: The highest frequency of gr/gr deletion carriers (6.8%, n = 6/88) was detected in cryptozoospermia cases (sperm count > 0–1 × 106/ejaculate).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study data.

claim: All 10 reference men with the gr/gr deletion and available andrological data were normozoospermic.
source: All 10 reference men with the gr/gr deletion and available andrological data were normozoospermic (220.3 [74.2–559.0] × 106 sperm/ejaculate).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's reference group data.

claim: The patient and reference groups exhibited similar prevalence of b2/b3 deletions (32.6% vs 32.4%).
source: The patient and the reference groups exhibited similar prevalence of b2/b3 deletions (388/1190, 32.6% vs 367/1134, 32.4%; Fisher's exact test, p=0.8).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the study showing no significant difference.

claim: There was a highly significant overrepresentation of Y chromosomes belonging to lineage R1a1-M458 in the gr/gr deletion carriers (22.7%) compared to the Estonian population frequency (5.1%).
source: Notably, there was a highly significant overrepresentation of Y chromosomes belonging to lineage R1a1-M458 in the gr/gr deletion carriers compared to the known Estonian population frequency (22.7% vs 5.1%; Fisher's exact test, p=5.3×10−4, OR = 5.5 [95% CI 2.2–13.7]; Figure 2B, Supplementary file 5; Underhill et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing study data to published population frequencies.

claim: Nearly all (99.4%) Estonian cases with the b2/b3 deletion belonged to the Y haplogroup N3.
source: Nearly all (99.4%) Estonian cases with the b2/b3 deletion belonged to the Y haplogroup N3, in which this event is fixed (Repping et al., 2004; Fernandes et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study data supported by citations.

claim: The expected retained copy number of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes consistent with the typical gr/gr deletion was found in 37/44 (~84%) cases.
source: The expected retained copy number of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes consistent with the typical gr/gr deletion, as determined by quantification using Droplet Digital PCR (ddPCR), was found in 37/44 (~84%) cases (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 2, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's gene dosage analysis.

claim: Three patients and three reference men carried a secondary b2/b4 duplication with no apparent effect on infertility status.
source: Three patients and three reference men carried a secondary b2/b4 duplication adding one or more amplicons of [two DAZ – two BPY2 – one CDY1] genes with no apparent effect on infertility status (Fisher's exact test, p=0.34).
evidence: This is a finding from the study showing no association with infertility.

claim: 78.5% of patients and 84.3% reference men with the b2/b3 deletion presented gene dosage consistent with the typical deletion.
source: Similarly, 78.5% of patients and 84.3% reference men with the b2/b3 deletion presented gene dosage consistent with the typical deletion (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 2, Supplementary files 7 and 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's gene dosage analysis.

claim: Secondary b2/b4 duplications were detected with significantly higher prevalence in patients (20.4%) compared to reference men (14.1%).
source: Although secondary b2/b4 duplications were detected with significantly higher prevalence in patients compared to the reference men (n = 78/382, 20.4% vs n = 35/249, 14.1%; Fisher's exact test, p=0.026, OR = 1.57 [95% CI 1.02–2.42]), no consistent effect of increased gene copy number on andrological parameters was observed (Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study comparing patient and control groups.

claim: No consistent effect of increased gene copy number on andrological parameters was observed for b2/b4 duplications.
source: Although secondary b2/b4 duplications were detected with significantly higher prevalence in patients compared to the reference men (n = 78/382, 20.4% vs n = 35/249, 14.1%; Fisher's exact test, p=0.026, OR = 1.57 [95% CI 1.02–2.42]), no consistent effect of increased gene copy number on andrological parameters was observed (Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analysis of andrological parameters.

claim: The dosage of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes does not play a major role in modulating the pathogenic effect of the gr/gr and b2/b3 deletions.
source: The data gathered from this analysis thus suggest that the dosage of DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 genes does not play a major role in modulating the pathogenic effect of the gr/gr and b2/b3 deletions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's gene dosage analysis.

claim: The major b2/b3 deletion subtype in both patients (99.7%) and reference cases (98.1%) was the loss of DAZ3-DAZ4-CDY1a genes.
source: The major b2/b3 deletion subtype in both patients (99.7%) and reference cases (98.1%) was the loss of DAZ3-DAZ4-CDY1a genes, whereas the most frequent gr/gr subtypes among all the deletion carriers were the loss of DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1a (41.9%, 18/43 cases) and DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1b (25.6%, 11/43 cases) combinations (Figure 2A, Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's deletion subtype analysis.

claim: The most frequent gr/gr subtypes were the loss of DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1a (41.9%) and DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1b (25.6%).
source: The major b2/b3 deletion subtype in both patients (99.7%) and reference cases (98.1%) was the loss of DAZ3-DAZ4-CDY1a genes, whereas the most frequent gr/gr subtypes among all the deletion carriers were the loss of DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1a (41.9%, 18/43 cases) and DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1b (25.6%, 11/43 cases) combinations (Figure 2A, Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's deletion subtype analysis.

claim: All five exons 7Y in the DAZ4 gene were missing in Y chromosomes with the DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1a deletion that had occurred in sub-lineages of the R1a1a1b1a2 haplogroup.
source: All five exons 7Y in the DAZ4 gene were missing in the Y chromosomes with the DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1a deletion that had occurred in sub-lineages of the R1a1a1b1a2 haplogroup (9/31 patients, 3/13 reference men), representing 12/18 DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1a deletion carriers.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's detailed genetic analysis of DAZ genes.

claim: The exon 7F in DAZ4 was lost in haplogroup I1 and its sub-lineages.
source: The exon 7F in DAZ4 was lost in haplogroup I1 and its sub-lineages (5/31, 2/13), that is 7/11 individuals carrying the DAZ1-DAZ2-CDY1b deletion (Supplementary files 10 and 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's detailed genetic analysis of DAZ genes.

claim: There was no evidence that loss of DAZ4 exons 7Y or 7F has any phenotypic consequences.
source: There was no evidence that loss of DAZ4 exons 7Y or 7F has any phenotypic consequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's phenotype analysis.

claim: Neither the loss of the DAZ1-DAZ2 nor the DAZ3-DAZ4 gene pair, combined with either a CDY1a or CDY1b gene, directly causes spermatogenic failure.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that neither the loss of the DAZ1-DAZ2 nor the DAZ3-DAZ4 gene pair, combined with either a CDY1a or CDY1b gene, directly causes spermatogenic failure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's analysis of deletion subtypes and phenotypes.

claim: No Y chromosomes were observed with fewer than two retained DAZ genes.
source: Interestingly, no Y chromosomes were observed with fewer than two retained DAZ genes.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's gene dosage analysis.

claim: Eight patients and two reference cases with a gr/gr deletion were missing DAZ2-DAZ4 genes.
source: Eight patients and two reference cases with a gr/gr deletion were missing DAZ2-DAZ4 genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's deletion subtype analysis.

claim: All but one subject with the atypical pair of lost DAZ genes (DAZ2-DAZ4 or DAZ1-DAZ3) belonged to the Y haplogroup R1a1-M458 and its sub-lineages.
source: All but one subject with this atypical pair of lost DAZ genes belonged to the Y haplogroup R1a1-M458 and its sub-lineages, significantly enriched in gr/gr deletion carriers (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's haplogroup analysis.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for the simultaneous deletion of either DAZ1-DAZ3 or DAZ2-DAZ4 genes is a preceding ~1.6 Mb long inversion between the r2 and r3 amplicons.
source: The most parsimonious explanation to explain the simultaneous deletion of either DAZ1-DAZ3 or DAZ2-DAZ4 genes is a preceding ~1.6 Mb long inversion between the r(ed)two and r(ed)three amplicons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data and structural analysis.

claim: The r2/r3 inversion almost completely loses the largest palindrome P1 and greatly expands the size of palindrome P2.
source: In r2/r3 inversion chromosomes, the largest palindrome P1 is almost completely lost and the size of the palindrome P2 is greatly expanded by positioning the homologous g1/g2 segments in an inverted orientation.
evidence: This is a structural analysis based on the inferred genomic rearrangement.

claim: The r2/r3 inversion is expected to destabilize the AZFc region as several long DNA amplicons with highly homologous DNA sequence are positioned in the same sequence orientation.
source: The r2/r3 inversion is consequently expected to destabilize the AZFc region as several long DNA amplicons with highly homologous DNA sequence are positioned in the same sequence orientation (b2, b3, and b4; g2 and g3; y1 and y3).
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on genomic structure.

claim: The detected r2/r3 inversion must have occurred only once in the common ancestor of R1a1-M458 sub-lineages.
source: Since these atypical deletion subtypes were identified only in a specific Y-chromosomal haplogroup, the detected r2/r3 inversion must have occurred only once in the common ancestor of R1a1-M458 sub-lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Among the analyzed 2324 men, 13 cases (0.6%) had the complex AZFc rearrangement combining r2/r3 inversion with a subsequent deletion.
source: Among the analyzed 2324 men, 13 cases with the complex AZFc rearrangement combining r2/r3 inversion with a subsequent deletion (from here on referred to as 'r2/r3 inversion plus deletion' for simplicity), represented 0.6% (Table 3).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study data.

claim: Approximately one in ten chromosomes with the r2/r3 inversion had undergone a subsequent deletion event (13/119, 11%).
source: Thus, approximately one in ten chromosomes with the r2/r3 inversion had undergone a subsequent deletion event (13/119, 11%).
evidence: This is a calculation based on study data and population frequency estimates.

claim: Idiopathic infertility cases carrying the r2/r3 inversion plus deletion exhibited extremely low sperm counts (median 2.0 × 106/ejaculate) compared to subjects without any AZFc deletions (median 12.5 × 106/ejaculate).
source: Idiopathic infertility cases carrying the r2/r3 inversion plus deletion in the AZFc region (n = 10) exhibited extremely low sperm counts compared to subjects without any AZFc deletions (median 2.0 vs 12.5 × 106/ejaculate; Wilcoxon test, nominal p=0.011) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the study's phenotype analysis.

claim: Nine of 10 men with r2/r3 inversion plus deletion showed severe spermatogenic failure (total sperm counts <10 × 106/ejaculate).
source: Nine of 10 men showed severe spermatogenic failure (total sperm counts <10 × 106/ejaculate), either azoospermia (n = 1), cryptozoospermia (n = 3), or severe oligozoospermia (n = 5) (Supplementary files 11 and 12).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's phenotype analysis.

claim: There was a highly significant enrichment of r2/r3 inversion plus deletion in men with severe spermatogenic failure (1.7%) compared to the rest (0.2%).
source: When all the men with andrological data (n = 2000) were stratified based on sperm counts, there was a highly significant enrichment of r2/r3 inversion plus deletion in men with severe spermatogenic failure (sperm counts 0–10 × 106) compared to the rest (1.7% vs 0.2%, Fisher's exact test, p=6.0×10−4, OR = 8.6 [95% CI 2.3–31.8]; Table 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's association analysis.

claim: Among carriers of Y lineage R1a1-M458, 33.7% of men with sperm counts 0–10 × 106 had undergone a subsequent AZFc partial deletion, compared to 4.0% with sperm counts >10 × 106.
source: Among carriers of this Y lineage, 33.7% of men with sperm counts 0–10 × 106 (9/27), but only 4.0% with sperm counts of >10 × 106 (3/72) had undergone a subsequent AZFc partial deletion (Fisher's exact test, p=3.0×10−4, OR = 12.0 [95% CI 2.9–48.9]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's subgroup analysis.

claim: The re-sequenced retained DAZ1-4, BPY2, and CDY1-2 genes were characterized by extremely low nucleotide variability in all Y-chromosomal lineages and deletion subtypes.
source: The re-sequenced retained DAZ1-4, BPY2, and CDY1-2 genes were characterized by extremely low nucleotide variability in all Y-chromosomal lineages and deletion subtypes (Supplementary file 13).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's sequencing analysis.

claim: For 476 re-sequenced samples, a total of 42 variants were identified with median 0.8 variants/kb and maximum two variants per individual.
source: For 476 samples (gr/gr, n = 40; b2/b3, n = 436), re-sequenced for the >94 kb region using Illumina MiSeq, a total of 42 variants were identified with median 0.8 variants/kb and maximum two variants per individual.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's sequencing analysis.

claim: The CDY2a-CDY2b genes harbored only one variable site.
source: The CDY2a-CDY2b genes harbored only one variable site, whereas DAZ1-DAZ2 carried 24 or 26 SNVs/indels.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's sequencing analysis.

claim: There was no evidence that the sequence variation in DAZ, BPY2, and CDY genes has any effect on infertility related parameters.
source: There was thus no evidence that the sequence variation in DAZ, BPY2, and CDY genes has any effect on infertility related parameters in the subjects examined.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analysis of sequence variation and phenotypes.

claim: Concordant with reports from other European populations, the gr/gr, but not the b2/b3 deletion, is a risk factor for spermatogenic impairment in Estonian men with >2-fold increased susceptibility to infertility.
source: Concordant with the reports from other European populations, the gr/gr, but not the b2/b3 deletion, is a risk factor for spermatogenic impairment in Estonian men with >2-fold increased susceptibility to infertility (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study comparing findings to published literature.

claim: The study uncovered complex AZFc rearrangements within Y haplogroup R1a1-M458 causing severe spermatogenic failure in the majority of carriers.
source: As a novel finding, the study uncovered complex AZFc rearrangements within a specific Y haplogroup, R1a1-M458 and its sub-lineages, causing severe spermatogenic failure in the majority of carriers (Figure 3, Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Y lineage R1a1-M458 has undergone a ~1.6 Mb r2/r3 inversion in the AZFc region that has disrupted the structure of palindromes P1 and P2.
source: This Y lineage has undergone a ~1.6 Mb r2/r3 inversion in the AZFc region that has disrupted the structure of the palindromes P1 and P2, promoting subsequent recurrent deletions and consequently, severely impaired the process of spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's structural and phenotypic analysis.

claim: The 44 detected gr/gr deletions were estimated to have originated independently at least 26 times across the Y phylogenetic tree.
source: The 44 detected gr/gr deletions in our study sample were estimated to have originated independently at least 26 times across the Y phylogenetic tree and include seven different combinations of DAZ and CDY1 gene losses.
evidence: This is an estimate based on phylogenetic and genetic analysis.

claim: One in four Estonian gr/gr deletion carriers belonged to Y-chromosomal haplogroup R1a1-M458.
source: Unexpectedly, one in four Estonian gr/gr deletion carriers belonged to the Y-chromosomal haplogroup R1a1-M458 (and its sub-lineages) (Figure 2A,B; 22.7% vs 5.1% reported as the Estonian population frequency; Underhill et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study data.

claim: A previous study reported a significant enrichment of haplogroup R1a among gr/gr-deleted chromosomes in the Polish population.
source: Notably, a previous study has reported a significant enrichment of the haplogroup R1a (ancestral lineage to the R1a1-M458) among gr/gr-deleted chromosomes in the Polish population (Rozen et al., 2012), which has a high prevalence, 25%, of R1a1-M458 (Underhill et al., 2015; Figure 4A, Supplementary file 15).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The r2/r3 inversion disrupts the structure of palindrome P1 and expands the size of the P2 palindrome more than twofold.
source: In contrast, the r2/r3 inversion disrupts the structure of palindrome P1 and expands the size of the P2 palindrome more than twofold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a structural analysis based on the inferred genomic rearrangement.

claim: The critical role of intact P1–P2 palindromes in the AZFc structure is supported by the observation that no Y chromosomes have been described with a single DAZ gene copy.
source: The critical role of intact P1–P2 palindromes in the AZFc structure is supported by the observation that no Y chromosomes have been described with a single DAZ gene copy, whereas the inverted DAZ gene pairs form the 'heart' of both P1 and P2.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed data and structural knowledge.

claim: The r2/r3 inversion plus deletion may predispose to spermatogenic impairment through substantial destabilization of the intra-chromosomal structure affecting meiotic recombination and chromosomal segregation.
source: As a likely scenario, the r2/r3 inversion plus deletion may predispose to spermatogenic impairment through substantial destabilization of the intra-chromosomal structure affecting meiotic recombination and chromosomal segregation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: Among 12 Estonian subjects carrying the AZFc r2/r3 inversion plus deletions with available sperm count data, nine cases exhibited severe spermatogenic failure, two cases had moderate oligozoospermia, and only one case was normozoospermic.
source: Among 12 Estonian subjects carrying the AZFc r2/r3 inversion plus deletions and with available data for sperm counts, nine cases exhibited severe spermatogenic failure, two cases had moderate oligozoospermia, and only one case (aged 18 years) was normozoospermic (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's phenotype analysis.

claim: This genetic effect was observed specifically on the effectiveness of spermatogenesis, whereas measurements of bitesticular volume and reproductive hormone levels did not stand out among the rest of analyzed infertile men.
source: This genetic effect was observed specifically on the effectiveness of spermatogenesis, whereas the measurements of bitesticular volume and reproductive hormone levels did not stand out among the rest of analyzed infertile men.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's phenotype analysis.

claim: No other Y-lineage-specific risk variants for spermatogenic impairment have been reported so far.
source: To our knowledge, no other Y-lineage-specific risk variants for spermatogenic impairment have been reported so far.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on literature knowledge.

claim: The DAZ2–DAZ4 deletion had been shown as a high-risk factor for male infertility in the Tunisian population.
source: Previously, the DAZ2–DAZ4 deletion had been shown as a high-risk factor for male infertility in the Tunisian population, but the Y haplogroups of those subjects were not investigated (Ghorbel et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In Northern and Central Europe, the prevalence of R1a1-M458 haplogroup ranges from ~1% in the Netherlands and Denmark to ~2–5% in Austria, Hungary, Germany, Baltics, and most Balkan countries.
source: In Northern and Central Europe, the prevalence of R1a1-M458 haplogroup carrying the r2/r3 inversion ranges from ~1% in the Netherlands and Denmark to ~2–5% in Austria, Hungary, Germany, Baltics, and most Balkan countries, whereas it is widespread in Slavic populations and carried by 12–26% of men (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 15; Underhill et al., 2015).
evidence: This prevalence data is supported by citations and shown in figures.

claim: R1a1-M458 is widespread in Slavic populations and carried by 12–26% of men.
source: In Northern and Central Europe, the prevalence of R1a1-M458 haplogroup carrying the r2/r3 inversion ranges from ~1% in the Netherlands and Denmark to ~2–5% in Austria, Hungary, Germany, Baltics, and most Balkan countries, whereas it is widespread in Slavic populations and carried by 12–26% of men (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 15; Underhill et al., 2015).
evidence: This prevalence data is supported by citations and shown in figures.

claim: In non-European populations, R1a1-M458 Y chromosomes are virtually non-existent.
source: In non-European populations, the R1a1-M458 Y chromosomes are virtually non-existent (for details, see Underhill et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: In some European populations, recurrent secondary AZFc partial deletions on R1a1-M458 chromosomes may potentially explain from 0.3% up to ~9% of cases presenting severe spermatogenic impairment.
source: However, in some European populations, recurrent secondary AZFc partial deletions on Y chromosomes representing the R1a1-M458 haplogroup (and its sub-lineages) may potentially explain from 0.3% up to ~9% of cases presenting severe spermatogenic impairment (sperm counts < 10 million per ejaculate) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an estimate based on population frequencies and study findings.

claim: The increased prevalence of either gr/gr or b2/b3 deletions in infertility cases appears to be population-dependent.
source: The evidence from the literature has shown that the increased prevalence of either gr/gr or b2/b3 deletions in infertility cases appears to be population-dependent (Bansal et al., 2016a; Bansal et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The largest study of Y-chromosomal phylogeny of gr/gr deletion carriers included 152 infertile subjects representing seven countries.
source: So far, the largest study of the Y-chromosomal phylogeny of gr/gr deletion carriers included 152 infertile subjects representing seven countries with different population genetic structures (Krausz et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Deep re-sequencing revealed that neither the dosage, sequence variation, nor exact copy of the retained DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 gene showed any detectable effect on spermatogenic parameters.
source: In addition to the main finding, our deep re-sequencing dataset revealed that neither the dosage, sequence variation, nor exact copy of the retained DAZ, BPY2, and CDY1 gene showed any detectable effect on spermatogenic parameters.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's comprehensive genetic analysis.

claim: All chromosomes with AZFc partial deletions exhibit extremely low overall sequence variation of the retained DAZ, BPY2, and CDY genes.
source: All chromosomes with AZFc partial deletions exhibit extremely low overall sequence variation of the retained DAZ, BPY2, and CDY genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's sequencing analysis.

claim: This observation is consistent with previous reports showing low levels of genetic diversity of the human Y chromosome.
source: This observation is consistent with previous reports showing low levels of genetic diversity of the human Y chromosome (Jobling and Tyler-Smith, 2017) and suggesting that novel variants may be rapidly removed by active gene conversion among Y-chromosomal duplicate genes or selective constraint (Hallast et al., 2013; Rozen et al., 2003; Trombetta and Cruciani, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Among the re-sequenced 382 chromosomes with b2/b3 deletions, no pathogenic mutations were detected in the single retained BPY2 and CDY1 gene copies.
source: Among the re-sequenced 382 chromosomes with b2/b3 deletions, no pathogenic mutations were detected in the single retained BPY2 and CDY1 gene copies.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's sequencing analysis.

claim: One in five or six Estonian Y chromosomes with gr/gr and b2/b3 deletions had undergone secondary rearrangements with no apparent effect on tested andrological parameters and fertility potential.
source: One in five or six Estonian Y chromosomes with gr/gr and b2/b3 deletions had undergone secondary rearrangements with no apparent effect on tested andrological parameters and fertility potential (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's structural analysis.

claim: Further copy number reductions beyond the initial gr/gr or b2/b3 deletion appear to be very rare.
source: However, further copy number reductions in this genomic region appear to be very rare – none of the 44 gr/gr or 631 b2/b3 deletion carriers were identified with further reductions beyond what is expected from the initial deletion.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's gene dosage analysis.

claim: The current study is the largest and most detailed to date in terms of both the number of patients with spermatogenic impairment and reference samples with available andrological data from a single population.
source: The current study is the largest and most detailed to date in terms of both the number of patients with spermatogenic impairment and reference samples with available andrological data from a single population, and detailed characterization of the genetic diversity of the AZFc region and phylogenetic background of the Y chromosomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design and scope.

claim: The study uncovered high levels of structural variation in the AZFc locus, but low sequence diversity of the coding genes within the region.
source: In summary, we have undertaken a comprehensive study of the carriers of AZFc partial gr/gr and b2/b3 deletions and uncovered high levels of structural variation in the AZFc locus, but low sequence diversity of the coding genes within the region.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Men carrying Y chromosomes with r2/r3 inversion plus deletion have >10 fold increased risk of severe spermatogenic failure.
source: Men carrying Y chromosomes with this complex rearrangement have >10 fold increased risk of severe spermatogenic failure, but the consequences of this risk could potentially be alleviated by early identification of the variant carriers and facilitating the storage of their sperm samples.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's association analysis.

claim: The study results have the potential to improve clinical diagnostics and management of idiopathic impaired spermatogenesis in a significant fraction of men originating from Northern and Central European populations.
source: Our study results thus have the potential to improve clinical diagnostics and management of idiopathic impaired spermatogenesis in a significant fraction of men originating from Northern and Central European populations.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical implications of the findings.

claim: The study analyzed 2324 Estonian men in total.
source: In analysing 2324 Estonian men, we uncovered a novel structural variant as a high-penetrance risk factor for male infertility.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample size.

claim: The study included 1190 patients with idiopathic infertility with sperm counts 0–39 × 106/ejaculate.
source: Included cases showed reduced sperm counts (<39 × 106/ejaculate) in at least two consecutive semen analyses (World Health Organization, 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the patient inclusion criteria.

claim: For all 2324 study subjects, complete AZFa, AZFb, and AZFc deletions were excluded.
source: For all 2324 study subjects, complete AZFa, AZFb, and AZFc deletions were excluded.
evidence: This is a description of the study exclusion criteria.

claim: The partial AZFc deletions identified were gr/gr (n = 46), b2/b3 (n = 756), and b1/b3 (n = 1).
source: The partial AZFc deletions identified using the STS-based polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays were gr/gr (n = 46), b2/b3 (n = 756), and b1/b3 (n = 1, reference case) (Table 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the detected deletions in the study.

claim: The most commonly detected N3 sub-lineage was N3a3a-L550 (~51% of 436 typed chromosomes).
source: The most commonly detected sub-lineage was N3a3a-L550 (~51% of 436 typed chromosomes) and in total 15 different haplogroups that had diverged after the b2/b3 deletion event in the common ancestor of N3 were present in Estonian men (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's haplogroup analysis.

claim: In total 15 different N3 haplogroups that had diverged after the b2/b3 deletion event were present in Estonian men.
source: The most commonly detected sub-lineage was N3a3a-L550 (~51% of 436 typed chromosomes) and in total 15 different haplogroups that had diverged after the b2/b3 deletion event in the common ancestor of N3 were present in Estonian men (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's haplogroup analysis.

claim: The AZFc region contains at least one multicopy family of non-coding RNA genes, TTTY4, with testis-enriched expression.
source: The AZFc region contains at least one multicopy family of non-coding RNA genes, TTTY4 (Testis-Specific Transcript, Y-Linked 4) with testis-enriched expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic content of the AZFc region based on established knowledge.

claim: TTTY4 genes are located in the three g1–g3 duplicons flanking the P1 and P2 palindromic 'hearts'.
source: These genes are located in the three g1–g3 duplicons flanking the P1 and P2 palindromic 'hearts'.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic location of TTTY4 genes.
